connection: Session 06 created Address, Employee, and an open ClockEntry with EmployeeId and ClockIn. ClockEntry cannot be completed or calculate duration yet. Extend the production models with initialization guarantees, nullable clock-out state, and completion invariants.
objectives: Distinguish a nullable property that models a real absent state (ClockOut) from one that is simply under-initialized (EmployeeDto.Name).
Explain how a private setter plus a nullable type together model "not yet clocked out".
Read and reproduce the real CS8618 warning on EmployeeDto.
Handle a nullable ClockEntry? return value safely, matching IClockEntryRepository.GetClockEntry.

visuals.title: Nullable means value or no value
visuals.explanation: DateTime? ClockOut explicitly permits either a real clock-out timestamp or null; every reader of ClockOut must account for both.

visuals.title: Construction guards required state
visuals.explanation: ClockEntry assigns EmployeeId and ClockIn in the constructor, so every successfully created object satisfies those requirements immediately.

visuals.title: The compiler flags an unproven guarantee
visuals.explanation: EmployeeDto.Name has no default and no constructor, so under Nullable enable the compiler raises CS8618: it cannot prove Name is non-null when the object is used.

visuals.title: A nullable return value forces a branch
visuals.explanation: IClockEntryRepository.GetClockEntry returns ClockEntry?, so ClockEntryService.Clockout must check for null before calling ClockOutEmployee.

preQuiz.explanation: The model owns the state transition.

concept.title: Required state belongs in construction
paragraphs: Employee identity and ClockEntry clock-in time are required from the moment each object exists. Constructors make that requirement unavoidable.
A nullable member should represent genuinely optional state, not unfinished initialization.
concept.code: public DateTime? ClockOut { get; private set; }

concept.title: Flow analysis follows the null check
paragraphs: Before clock-out, ClockOut is null. After a guard proves it has a value, the completed path can safely use ClockOut.Value.
The compiler tracks that proof through the local control flow; it does not guess business intent.

concept.title: Invariants reject impossible transitions
paragraphs: Clock-out cannot precede clock-in, and a completed entry cannot be completed again. Those are ClockEntry rules, so ClockEntry protects them.
Callers do not need to remember a fragile sequence of property assignments.

reflections: Which ClockEntry values are required versus only-sometimes-present, and why?
What does the compiler's CS8618 warning prove, and what does it not prove?
Why is GetClockEntry's nullable return type paired with a thrown exception one level up, in ClockEntryService.Clockout?
whatBreaks: Making ClockOut's setter public lets any code close an entry without going through ClockOutEmployee, silently breaking the double-clock-out guard. Removing EmployeeDto's pragma reintroduces CS8618, which fails the build under this course's TreatWarningsAsErrors setting. Removing the null check in Clockout turns a legitimate "not clocked in" case into a NullReferenceException that hides the real problem.
summary: Nullable annotations describe permitted absence -- ClockEntry.ClockOut and IClockEntryRepository.GetClockEntry's return type both use DateTime?/ClockEntry? to make "not yet" part of the type, not a convention. EmployeeDto shows the same analysis catching an under-proven guarantee as a real compiler warning, CS8618, rather than a runtime surprise.
